Scope

The present review surveys a body of 104 papers dealing with catalysts for carbon dioxide hydrogenation that have appeared in the literature over the last 7 years. Carbon dioxide hydrogenation, for those approaching the topic for the first time, may be understood as the reaction of carbon dioxide with hydrogen over a solid catalyst, a reaction which yields a range of products including, among others, methanol, methane, and carbon monoxide. The papers encompassed by the set report, in varying degrees of detail, the preparation of catalysts, their testing in continuous reactors, and the distributions of products obtained under the conditions stated by the authors. The scope of the set is restricted to heterogeneous catalysts for which carbon dioxide figures as the reactant under study; papers concerned with electrochemical conversion and papers concerned with photochemical conversion consequently fall outside it, as do papers in which carbon dioxide appears merely as an impurity in the feed. Studies of the reverse water-gas shift reaction are included where that reaction forms part of a broader hydrogenation scheme, and excluded in those cases where carbon monoxide is the only intended product and no hydrogenation step ensues. The review is organised in four parts, addressing in turn the scope of the set, the results which the set may be said to support, the points on which the reports are in conflict, and the measurements which the set does not contain. It should be emphasised that conditions vary very considerably from paper to paper, in pressure, in temperature, and in feed proportions, and the review accordingly compares reports in terms of the quantities the papers themselves state, rather than attempting any reduction to a common basis which the underlying papers do not share.

Established results

Copper-based catalysts constitute by far the most extensively reported family where the formation of methanol is concerned. The standard preparation is one in which copper is carried on zinc oxide, with alumina additionally present as a structural component serving to keep the copper in a dispersed state. Activity is found to track the exposed copper surface, in the sense that preparations which succeed in dispersing the copper more finely also convert more carbon dioxide per unit mass of catalyst, a relationship which appears to hold both across different preparations and across different laboratories. The reverse water-gas shift reaction proceeds in parallel wherever carbon dioxide and hydrogen are brought into contact with the catalyst, and carbon monoxide is accordingly found in the product of every methanol catalyst in the set. The proportion of carbon monoxide rises with temperature, while methanol selectivity falls as temperature rises, reflecting the fact that the shift reaction is favoured at higher temperatures whereas methanol formation is favoured at lower ones. Water, which is a product of both reactions, acts to inhibit the methanol reaction: rates are observed to fall as water accumulates, and arrangements in which water is removed between stages achieve correspondingly higher conversions. Oxide supports, it emerges, are by no means inert carriers, since the boundary between the metal and the oxide is the site to which a large part of the activity is attributed, and substituting zirconium oxide for zinc oxide changes activity and selectivity alike for one and the same metal. Indium oxide catalysts deliver high methanol selectivity accompanied by little methane, and display a resistance to the loss of surface which afflicts copper at temperature, although their activity per unit mass falls below that of the copper preparations in most reports. Nickel-based catalysts, for their part, carry the reaction through to methane and convert carbon dioxide almost completely under conditions where the methanol catalysts produce mixtures, so that the set divides along the lines of the intended product. Promoters introduced in small amounts are found to alter selectivity to a greater extent than they alter activity. Deactivation in the tests reported is dominated by the growth of the metal particles together with the action of the water formed in the reaction, two effects which the set rarely manages to separate.

Disagreements

Considerable disagreement exists in the literature with respect to the selectivity to methanol at a stated conversion, in the case of copper-based catalysts operated under conditions which the respective reports describe as comparable. One and the same preparation is reported as exhibiting quite different selectivities by different groups, the discrepancy comfortably exceeding the spread reported within any single study. One school of reporting attributes the selectivity to the size of the copper particles, maintaining that smaller particles afford the higher selectivity and that preparations are therefore to be ranked by particle size alone. A second school attributes the selectivity to the boundary subsisting between the copper and the oxide, ranking preparations instead by the extent of that boundary, with particle size entering the picture only in so far as it modifies the boundary. Since the two rankings order the selfsame preparations differently, and since the papers themselves do not resolve the question of which quantity the selectivity in fact follows, the matter must be regarded as open. Disagreement extends, furthermore, to the action of water. In one body of reports the inhibition exerted by water is portrayed as kinetic and reversible, the rate recovering once the water is removed, whereas in another body of reports the loss is portrayed as permanent, the water being held responsible for changing the catalyst itself in the course of a run. The distinction is far from academic, inasmuch as the two accounts point towards quite different reactor arrangements, namely staged beds with intermediate water removal in the one case and a catalyst selected for its ability to withstand water in the other. Neither conflict can be resolved from the set as published, for the simple reason that the papers state their conditions in forms which do not carry across from one report to another: conversion is quoted at differing positions within the bed, and selectivity is in many instances not quoted at a stated conversion at all.

Gaps

Perhaps the most striking omission in the set is that no paper in it reports conversion after extended time on stream. The measurement which nobody reports is, in other words, the activity of the catalyst following operation of a duration sufficient for deactivation, rather than initial activity, to become the governing factor in performance: the tests in the set are terminated while the catalyst remains close to its initial state, and such deactivation as the established results describe is inferred on the basis of short runs and post-mortem examination rather than measured over the run itself. The omission extends also to the feed employed. The papers test clean feeds composed of carbon dioxide and hydrogen, and no paper reports performance over time on a feed bearing the impurities characteristic of a captured industrial stream, notwithstanding that a catalyst in actual service would inevitably encounter such a feed. Regeneration fares no better: a handful of papers mention in passing that a catalyst was regenerated, yet none reports the activity thereby recovered, the number of cycles the catalyst is capable of withstanding, or the selectivity obtaining after regeneration. Carbon balances, moreover, are incomplete in a substantial part of the set, with the result that the fate of such carbon as does not appear among the stated products cannot be verified from the papers. The set accordingly supports comparisons between fresh catalysts operating under clean conditions, but does not support the comparison upon which an industrial selection would properly rest, namely performance sustained over time, on a realistic feed, following regeneration.

Scope

The review covers 104 papers on catalysts for carbon dioxide hydrogenation published in the last 7 years. Carbon dioxide hydrogenation is the reaction of carbon dioxide with hydrogen over a solid catalyst, giving products that include methanol, methane, and carbon monoxide. The papers in the set report catalyst preparation, tests in continuous reactors, and the product distributions the catalysts give under stated conditions. The set is limited to heterogeneous catalysts tested with carbon dioxide as the reactant under study. Papers on electrochemical conversion and papers on photochemical conversion fall outside the set, as do papers in which carbon dioxide appears only as a feed impurity. Studies of the reverse water-gas shift reaction are included where that reaction is reported as part of a hydrogenation scheme, and excluded where carbon monoxide is the sole intended product and no hydrogenation step follows. The review is organised in four parts: the scope of the set, the results the set supports, the points on which reports conflict, and the measurements the set does not contain. Conditions differ widely across the set, in pressure, in temperature, and in the proportions of the feed. The review therefore compares reports on the quantities the papers themselves state, and does not reduce results to a common basis the papers do not share. Papers are grouped in the review by the catalyst family they report rather than by the preparation in full, because preparations recur across papers with variations in detail that the review does not track. Methanol is the product aim of the largest part of the set, methane of a smaller part, and carbon monoxide of the remainder, where the shift reaction is studied for its own sake or as the first stage of a longer chain. A paper is counted once, under the product its authors state as the aim, where a paper reports more than one product.

Established results

Copper-based catalysts are the most reported family for the formation of methanol. The standard preparation carries copper on zinc oxide, with alumina present as a structural component that holds the copper dispersed. Activity tracks the exposed copper surface: preparations that disperse the copper more finely convert more carbon dioxide per unit mass of catalyst, and the relation holds across preparations and across laboratories. The reverse water-gas shift reaction runs in parallel wherever carbon dioxide and hydrogen meet the catalyst, and carbon monoxide appears in the product of every methanol catalyst in the set. The share of carbon monoxide rises with temperature, and methanol selectivity falls as temperature rises, because the shift reaction is favoured at the higher temperature while methanol formation is favoured at the lower. Water is a product of both reactions and inhibits the methanol reaction: rates fall as water accumulates, and reactor arrangements that remove water between stages raise the conversion reached. Oxide supports are not inert carriers. The boundary between the metal and the oxide is the site to which much of the activity is assigned, and changing the oxide from zinc oxide to zirconium oxide changes both activity and selectivity for the same metal. Indium oxide catalysts give high methanol selectivity with little methane, and resist the loss of surface that copper suffers at temperature; their activity per unit mass is lower than that of the copper preparations in most reports. Nickel-based catalysts take the reaction to methane and convert carbon dioxide nearly completely under conditions where the methanol catalysts give mixtures, so the set divides by the intended product. Promoters added in small amounts change selectivity more than they change activity. Conversion rises with pressure, because methanol formation reduces the number of gas molecules as it proceeds while the shift reaction does not; pressure therefore acts on selectivity as well as on conversion, and the higher pressures in the set are reported with the higher methanol selectivities. Feeds richer in hydrogen raise conversion on all families in the set, and on the methanation catalysts a hydrogen-rich feed is the normal condition reported. The preparation most reported for the copper family is coprecipitation, and preparations made by other routes are usually reported against a coprecipitated standard, which gives the set a common reference even where conditions differ. Deactivation in the tests reported is dominated by growth of the metal particles and by the action of the water formed, and the two are rarely separated in the set.

Disagreements

Reports conflict on the selectivity to methanol at a stated conversion, for copper-based catalysts run under conditions the reports describe as comparable. The same preparation is reported with different selectivities by different groups, and the difference is larger than the spread within any one report. One line of reports assigns the selectivity to the size of the copper particles: smaller particles are said to give the higher selectivity, and preparations are then ranked by particle size alone. A second line assigns the selectivity to the boundary between copper and oxide, and ranks preparations by the extent of that boundary, with particle size entering only as it changes the boundary. The two rankings order the same preparations differently, and the papers do not settle which quantity the selectivity follows. Reports also conflict on the action of water. In one set of reports the inhibition by water is kinetic and reversible: remove the water and the rate returns. In another set the loss is permanent, and the water is held to change the catalyst itself over the course of a run. The conflict matters because the two accounts prescribe different reactor arrangements, staged beds with water removal in the first case and a catalyst chosen to withstand water in the second. Reports conflict further on the part played by alumina in the standard copper preparation. In one account the alumina is a structural component only, present to hold the copper dispersed and taking no part in the reaction. In another account the alumina is held to enter the working surface and to contribute to the adsorption of carbon dioxide, so that removing it changes the chemistry and not only the texture of the catalyst. The preparations compared in the two accounts differ in more than the alumina content, and the set does not contain a comparison in which alumina alone is varied. Neither conflict is resolved by the set as published, because the papers state their conditions in forms that do not carry across reports: conversion is quoted at different positions in the bed, and selectivity is not always quoted at a stated conversion at all.

Gaps

No paper in the set reports conversion after extended time on stream. The measurement nobody reports is the activity of the catalyst after operation long enough for deactivation, rather than initial activity, to govern the performance: tests in the set end while the catalyst is still near its initial state, and the deactivation that the established results describe is inferred from short runs and from examination after the event, not measured over the run itself. The gap extends to the feed. Papers test clean feeds of carbon dioxide and hydrogen, and no paper reports performance over time on a feed carrying the impurities of a captured industrial stream, although the catalyst in service would meet such a feed. Regeneration is treated the same way: a few papers state that a catalyst was regenerated, and none reports the activity recovered, the number of cycles the catalyst withstands, or the selectivity after regeneration. Carbon balances are incomplete in much of the set, so the fate of the carbon that does not appear in the stated products cannot be checked from the papers. Characterisation in the set is of the fresh catalyst and of the spent catalyst after the run; no paper reports a measurement of the working surface made during the run itself, so the state of the catalyst at the moment its activity is quoted is inferred rather than observed. Start-up and shut-down are likewise absent: no paper reports what repeated cycling between reaction conditions and rest does to activity or to selectivity, although a catalyst in service on an intermittent renewable hydrogen supply would be cycled as a matter of routine. The set therefore supports the comparison of fresh catalysts under clean conditions, and does not support the comparison on which an industrial choice would rest: performance held over time, on a real feed, after regeneration.
